screens.title: Connecting Arduino to Raspberry Pi: Serial, I2C, and Bluetooth
screens.subtitle: Practical links, wiring, and simple protocol design for reliable IoT data exchange

narration.text: In many IoT systems the Arduino and Raspberry Pi are a team. The Arduino sits close to sensors and actuators and responds quickly. The Raspberry Pi runs higher level software, network services, and a user interface. In this chapter you will learn common ways to connect them: USB or UART serial for simple streams, I2C when the Pi is the master and the Arduino a slave, and Bluetooth serial modules for wireless links. We'll also build small message formats with delimiters and checksums so your data stays reliable across noisy links. You will see concrete examples you can copy: an Arduino sketch that sends labeled sensor readings, Python code on the Pi that parses those messages, and an I2C slave example that returns scaled sensor bytes on request. Understanding these patterns helps you choose the right link for short enclosed connections, PCB-mounted pairs, or untethered wireless setups. By the end you'll be ready to wire, configure, and design a simple protocol for a greenhouse or monitoring project. Which connection will you try first, USB serial or I2C?

keyIdea.title: Why connect both boards?
keyIdea.text: Use the Arduino for low-latency sensor work and the Raspberry Pi for networking and UI. Choose the physical link that fits distance, enclosure, and extension needs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives guide the hands-on and conceptual work in this chapter. First, you will establish serial communication between an Arduino and Raspberry Pi so the Pi can read labeled sensor strings and command actuators. That skill is practical because USB or UART is the fastest way to prototype a Pi–Arduino team: the Pi treats the Arduino as a serial device and you can parse simple key-value pairs. Second, you will configure I2C with the Pi as master and the Arduino as a slave. This teaches how to poll sensors or request single-byte values efficiently when boards are housed together. Third, you will learn how to use Bluetooth modules like the HC-05 to create wireless serial links; you will pair the module and use the Pi's serial interface to exchange messages. Fourth, you will design a message protocol that includes delimiters, checksums, and acknowledgments so transfers are robust. Each objective is a practical skill: wiring, configuration, small code snippets, and a checklist for protocol robustness that keeps your IoT data trustworthy and extendable.

screens.title: Why pair Arduino and Raspberry Pi?
screens.subtitle: Division of labor: edge device and edge gateway

narration.text: When you pair an Arduino and a Raspberry Pi you combine complementary strengths. The Arduino excels at real-time, low-level hardware tasks: reading analog sensors, debouncing switches, and driving PWM outputs. It is suited to deterministic loops and quick responses. The Raspberry Pi brings a full operating system, networking, storage, and a high-level language runtime. It hosts web servers, databases, and cloud connectors. Practically, this means you can let the Arduino sample sensors and handle immediate actuator timing while the Pi collects those readings, applies heavier processing, and provides a user-facing dashboard. For example, an Arduino can poll a temperature sensor every second and send labeled readings; the Pi can aggregate, time-stamp, and expose them via a local web page. A common misconception is that the Pi can replace an Arduino in every case. While a Pi can perform many tasks, it is not as predictable for strict timing under load unless you offload those tasks to a microcontroller. The takeaway is to match the job to the device: use Arduino for low-latency control and Pi for networking and UI. That design reduces complexity, improves reliability, and makes debugging clearer.

keyIdea.title: Match roles to strengths
keyIdea.text: Use Arduino for deterministic sensor and actuator work; use Raspberry Pi for networking, storage, and user interfaces.

content.html:
Definition

Edge device vs Edge gateway

A short definition and practical mapping to hardware tasks.

Arduino — Edge device
  • Real-time sampling and GPIO control
  • Low-latency actuator feedback
  • Simple serial output for transport
Raspberry Pi — Edge gateway
  • Runs Python services and web UIs
  • Handles network connectivity and storage
  • Parses, timestamps, and persists sensor streams
Key Takeaway

Split responsibilities: let the Arduino do time-sensitive I/O and the Pi handle higher-level logic and networking.

Analogy

Analogy: Sensor assistant and server

Think of the Arduino as an assistant who reads instruments and flips switches, and the Raspberry Pi as the server that stores results and shows them to visitors.

Concrete scenario
An Arduino reads temperature and light every second and sends labeled lines like TEMP:25.5 to the Pi. The Pi logs readings and serves them in a browser dashboard.
Common mistake
Putting all responsibilities on the Pi can make timing brittle and debugging harder when the OS schedules unpredictably.
Try this
Start by streaming one sensor label over serial and confirm the Pi prints the parsed number before adding more sensors.

screens.title: Serial over USB or UART
screens.subtitle: Stream labeled sensor lines and parse them with pyserial

narration.text: Serial communication is the easiest way to connect an Arduino to a Raspberry Pi. When you plug the Arduino into the Pi over USB it appears as a serial device such as /dev/ttyACM0 or /dev/ttyUSB0 and you can use Python's pyserial to read and write. The Arduino opens Serial at a baud rate and prints labeled lines like TEMP:VALUE followed by a newline. On the Pi, open the same baud on the serial device, read lines, and parse key-value pairs. A concrete example: an Arduino sketch reads analog A0, prints TEMP: and the value, then waits a second. The Pi script opens pyserial, flushes, and repeatedly reads lines, checking the prefix to extract the sensor value. A common misconception is to assume raw numbers are always aligned; newline-delimited labeled lines avoid ambiguity. When you need commands from the Pi to the Arduino, send labeled commands like CMD:LED_ON and handle ACK:OK responses. This simple command-reply convention is a robust starting point for bidirectional communication. Serial over USB or UART means use labeled, newline-terminated messages and acks so both sides can parse and confirm actions over usb or uart.. In practical terms, stream labeled sensor lines and parse them with pyserial. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Serial is simple and bidirectional
keyIdea.text: Use labeled, newline-terminated messages and ACKs so both sides can parse and confirm actions over USB or UART.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Arduino: serial output sketch

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
}

void loop() {
  int temp = analogRead(A0);
  Serial.print("TEMP:");
  Serial.println(temp);
  delay(1000);
}
Example format
TEMP:512 followed by newline. Labeling avoids ambiguity when multiple sensors stream.
Code Walkthrough

Raspberry Pi: pyserial reader

import serial
import time

ser = serial.Serial('/dev/ttyUSB0', 9600, timeout=1)
ser.flush()

while True:
    if ser.in_waiting > 0:
        line = ser.readline().decode('utf-8').rstrip()
        if line.startswith("TEMP:"):
            temp = int(line.split(":")[1])
            print(f"Temperature: {temp}")
    time.sleep(0.1)
Notes
  • Confirm the correct device node on the Pi before opening.
  • Use labeled prefixes so the parser can handle mixed messages.

screens.title: Command protocols and message formats
screens.subtitle: Build labels, delimiters, and ACKs for reliable parsing

narration.text: A clear message format prevents misinterpretation when streams mix sensor updates and commands. Start by choosing a start marker, stable separators, and an end marker or newline so the receiver can detect message boundaries. A simple and common pattern is prefix labels like TEMP:25.5 or CMD:LED_ON followed by a newline. For higher robustness add a start delimiter such as a dollar sign and a checksum field, for example: $TEMP,25.5,HUM,60.2,*CHECKSUM followed by newline. The checksum is computed over the payload and allows the receiver to detect corrupted messages. Use acknowledgments for commands: Pi sends CMD:LED_ON; Arduino replies ACK:OK after performing the action. Handle timeouts by retransmitting if no ACK arrives in a reasonable window. A misconception to avoid is relying on implicit boundaries like fixed timing; noise and buffering can re-synchronize differently. Concrete example: when the Arduino prints TEMP:25.5 you parse with labels; when using the delimited format include a checksum and verify it before applying changes. This design reduces misapplied commands on actuators and ensures data shown on dashboards is trustworthy. Command protocols and message formats means combine delimiters, checksums, and acks so messages are identified, validated, and confirmed before acting.. In practical terms, build labels, delimiters, and acks for reliable parsing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Format, verify, acknowledge
keyIdea.text: Combine delimiters, checksums, and ACKs so messages are identified, validated, and confirmed before acting.

content.html:
Process Flow

Designing a message protocol

1. Delimiters
Choose a start marker and end marker (or newline) so frames are detected reliably.
2. Labels
Use key-value pairs like TEMP, HUM so the parser knows which number maps to which sensor.
3. Checksum
Include a checksum to detect corruption, for example an XOR of payload bytes.
Example frame:
$TEMP,25.5,HUM,60.2,*5A
Here $ begins the frame, comma separates pairs, * starts the checksum and ends the frame.
ACK pattern
Pi sends CMD:LED_ON; Arduino performs and replies ACK:OK. If no ACK arrives, Pi may retry after a timeout.
Common mistake
Relying on timing instead of clear delimiters leads to misaligned reads when data bursts or buffering occurs.

screens.title: I2C: Pi as master, Arduino as slave
screens.subtitle: Poll the Arduino for scaled bytes and send commands without USB overhead

narration.text: I2C is useful when the Arduino and Raspberry Pi live close together, inside the same enclosure or on the same PCB. The Pi acts as the master and initiates reads and writes; the Arduino is a slave at a specific 7-bit address. This pattern avoids USB device nodes and gives you quick, byte-level exchanges. On the Arduino you register handlers for requests and receives, and return bytes when the Pi polls. A practical use is to scale an analog reading into a single byte and serve it with Wire. write so the Pi can read a compact sensor value frequently. Wiring requires shared SDA and SCL lines — typically to GPIO 2 and GPIO 3 on the Pi — plus a common ground. Remember to enable I2C on the Pi via raspi-config and install the smbus Python library. A common misconception is that I2C is plug-and-play at any distance: it is intended for short runs and shared bus topologies. If you need longer range, use serial or Bluetooth instead. The design gives tight polling control and low overhead for small, frequent reads.

keyIdea.title: I2C for short, efficient polls
keyIdea.text: Use I2C when boards are co-located and you want the Pi to poll for single-byte sensor values with minimal overhead.

content.html:
Architecture

I2C master-slave roles

The Pi starts transactions and the Arduino responds. Use it for compact, frequent reads without USB overhead.
Wiring
Connect SDA (GPIO 2, pin 3), SCL (GPIO 3, pin 5), and GND. Enable I2C in raspi-config.
Software
Install python3-smbus and use read_byte/write_byte to exchange single bytes with the slave address.
Key Takeaway

I2C is efficient for short, co-located connections and tight polling loops but not for long distances.

Example flow
Pi requests a byte; Arduino reads analog A0, scales to a byte and sends it back via Wire.write. Pi interprets the byte as the sensor value.
When to choose I2C
  • Boards share the same enclosure
  • Short wires and frequent polling
  • Need low overhead direct reads
Gotcha
I2C requires pull-ups and short wires; check address conflicts if multiple slaves are present.

screens.title: Arduino I2C slave sketch
screens.subtitle: Respond to requests and handle received commands

narration.text: On the Arduino side I2C needs a slave address and handlers for requests and receives. The example in the chapter sets the slave address to 0x04, scales an analog reading into a byte, and uses Wire. onRequest to write that byte when polled. It also watches Wire. onReceive to read incoming command bytes and toggle an LED accordingly. Practically, you will compile and upload this sketch to the Arduino, wire SDA, SCL, and ground to the Pi, then watch the Pi read bytes. A concrete code snippet shows the Wire. begin with the address, a loop that sets dataToSend to analogRead(A0) / 4 to scale 0–1023 into a byte, and a requestEvent that calls Wire. write. A common mistake is forgetting to scale analog values or not setting pins to outputs before toggling. Also be explicit about common ground between boards. When working through this on real hardware, verify the slave address and confirm that the Pi uses the same address in smbus calls to avoid read errors. Understanding the Arduino slave handlers gives you control over both data reporting and command handling on the bus.

keyIdea.title: Slave handlers
keyIdea.text: Use onRequest to send bytes and onReceive to accept commands so the Arduino can both report and act on bus messages.

content.html:
Arduino (I2C slave)
#include <Wire.h>
#define SLAVE_ADDRESS 0x04

byte dataToSend = 0;

void setup() {
  Wire.begin(SLAVE_ADDRESS);
  Wire.onRequest(requestEvent);
  Wire.onReceive(receiveEvent);
}

void loop() {
  dataToSend = analogRead(A0) / 4;  // Scale to byte
  delay(100);
}

void requestEvent() {
  Wire.write(dataToSend);
}

void receiveEvent(int bytes) {
  while (Wire.available()) {
    char c = Wire.read();
    if (c == '1') digitalWrite(13, HIGH);
    if (c == '0') digitalWrite(13, LOW);
  }
}
This sketch scales the analog input to a single byte and toggles pin 13 based on received characters.
Practical notes
  • Set the right slave address and avoid collisions on a shared bus.
  • Scale sensor values to fit the single-byte response when appropriate.
  • Remember a common ground and short SDA/SCL runs for reliability.
Check your understanding
If you read a byte of 200 from the Pi, what approximate analog value did the Arduino supply?

screens.title: Raspberry Pi I2C master (smbus)
screens.subtitle: Read bytes and write control codes from Python

narration.text: On the Raspberry Pi you use the smbus library to speak I2C as a master. After enabling I2C in raspi-config and installing Python three-smbus, create an SMBus object and read a byte from the slave address periodically. The chapter's example shows a loop that reads a byte and prints it, then writes a character to toggle an LED on the Arduino slave by sending ord('1') or ord('0'). This pattern is lightweight and efficient for short sensor values. A concrete example: bus. read_byte(SLAVE_ADDRESS) returns the scaled sensor value that the Arduino prepared, while bus. write_byte(SLAVE_ADDRESS, ord('1')) instructs the Arduino to set a digital pin high. Common problems include forgetting to enable I2C, using the wrong bus number (typically bus 1 on modern Pis), or addresses that collide. Always confirm wiring and run i2cdetect to see devices. The Pi can poll as fast as needed, but remember bus timing and give the Arduino time to update its sample to avoid reading stale measurements. This approach tightly integrates sensing and control on a single two-wire bus. Raspberry Pi I2C master (smbus) means use smbus to read bytes and write control bytes; check i2c enablement and bus/device addresses before polling.. In practical terms, read bytes and write control codes from python. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SMBus polling
keyIdea.text: Use smbus to read bytes and write control bytes; check I2C enablement and bus/device addresses before polling.

content.html:
Pi (I2C master)
import smbus
import time

bus = smbus.SMBus(1)
SLAVE_ADDRESS = 0x04

while True:
    data = bus.read_byte(SLAVE_ADDRESS)
    print(f"Sensor value: {data}")
    bus.write_byte(SLAVE_ADDRESS, ord('1'))  # Turn LED on
    time.sleep(1)
    bus.write_byte(SLAVE_ADDRESS, ord('0'))  # Turn LED off
    time.sleep(1)
Use i2cdetect and raspi-config to verify the bus and device before running the script.
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Is I2C enabled in raspi-config?
  • Are SDA/SCL and GND wired correctly and short?
  • Does i2cdetect show the slave address?
Pro tip
Use single-byte scaling for frequent polls and reserve multi-byte frames for less frequent, richer payloads.

screens.title: Bluetooth HC-05 pairing and serial use
screens.subtitle: Make the HC-05 appear as a serial port and use pyserial

narration.text: Bluetooth modules such as the HC-05 provide a wireless serial link between Arduino and Raspberry Pi. The HC-05 connects to Arduino RX/TX for serial IO and exposes a Bluetooth service that the Pi can pair with using the Pi's Bluetooth tools. The chapter lists the key steps: install bluetooth and blueman tools, put the HC-05 in AT mode to configure it when needed, then use bluetoothctl on the Pi to scan, pair, trust, and connect. After pairing the HC-05 typically appears as a serial device like /dev/rfcomm0 on the Pi and you can use pyserial exactly as you would with USB: open the port at the agreed baud and exchange labeled messages. A practical example is replacing a USB cable with HC-05 and testing that TEMP: and CMD: lines flow across the wireless link. Common pitfalls are forgetting to set the HC-05 baud or leaving it in AT mode unintentionally. Wireless links add potential interference and pairing steps, so choose Bluetooth when you need untethered communication and are comfortable with pairing and security considerations. Bluetooth HC-05 pairing and serial use means pair the hc-05 to the pi so it appears as a serial device; then exchange labeled messages using pyserial just like usb serial.. In practical terms, make the hc-05 appear as a serial port and use pyserial. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process

HC-05 pairing and usage

Steps
  1. Install bluetooth tools on Pi.
  2. Put HC-05 in AT mode to configure if needed.
  3. Use bluetoothctl to scan, pair, and trust the device.
  4. Connect and use /dev/rfcomm0 with pyserial.
Usage notes
Once connected, pyserial code is identical to USB serial. Verify baud matches the HC-05 configuration and the Arduino serial settings.
Concrete scenario: pair HC-05, open /dev/rfcomm0 on the Pi, and confirm the Arduino's TEMP: lines arrive without a USB cable.

screens.title: Choose the right link: USB serial vs I2C vs Bluetooth
screens.subtitle: Match the communication method to distance, latency, and complexity

narration.text: Choosing a transport depends on distance, enclosure, and how much overhead you accept. USB or UART serial is the fastest path to prototype: plug the Arduino into the Pi and use pyserial to read human-readable labeled lines. It is simple, works over modest cable lengths, and supports straightforward two-way commands. I2C is ideal when both boards are co-located inside an enclosure or on the same PCB; it offers low-overhead polling and compact single-byte transfers, but requires enabling I2C on the Pi and is sensitive to wire length and pull-ups. Bluetooth with an HC-05 adds wireless convenience but requires pairing, configuration, and is more exposed to interference; use it when untethered operation matters. A common misconception is that wireless always simplifies development — pairing and debugging can slow you down. For a greenhouse inside a single box, I2C or USB serial are the best choices. If you need remote placement across a room, Bluetooth or other wireless links make sense. The decision affects how you design message formats, error handling, and physical wiring. Choose the right link: USB serial vs I2C vs Bluetooth means pick usb serial for prototyping, i2c for short internal links, and bluetooth for untethered operation—each has trade-offs in setup and reliability.. In practical terms, match the communication method to distance, latency, and complexity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Select by constraints
keyIdea.text: Pick USB serial for prototyping, I2C for short internal links, and Bluetooth for untethered operation—each has trade-offs in setup and reliability.

content.html:
Comparison
USB / UART
Easy prototyping, two-way commands, works with pyserial. Best for initial builds and when cable length is short to moderate.
I2C
Low overhead for polling, Pi as master, Arduino as slave. Best inside the same enclosure or PCB; not for long distances.
Bluetooth (HC-05)
Wireless serial after pairing. Good when you must avoid cables, but introduces pairing and interference considerations.
Key Takeaway

Match transport to physical and latency constraints; design the same robust protocol on top regardless of link.

Misconception
Wireless is always better — not true. It increases setup steps and possible interference compared to wired links.

screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

First, serial over USB or UART provides the fastest prototype path: send labeled, newline-terminated messages and parse them with pyserial. Second, I2C is excellent for short, co-located boards where the Pi polls an Arduino slave for single-byte values using smbus. Third, Bluetooth modules like the HC-05 create wireless serial ports once paired, but require pairing steps and careful baud configuration. Each method benefits from a reliable message protocol with delimiters, checksums, and acknowledgments. Keep testing incrementally: verify single-message parsing before adding more sensors or command flows. These ideas will help you build a robust greenhouse monitor or similar IoT projects that need reliable, predictable data flow between microcontrollers and gateway systems. narration.text: Use this quick reference as you work through wiring and code. First, verify device nodes and bus addresses: check /dev entries for USB and rfcomm, and run i2cdetect for I2C. Second, always use labeled messages or frames with delimiters so your parser can recover from partial reads. Third, include a checksum or simple XOR over the payload to detect corruption and use ACK messages for commands to confirm actions. These habits reduce debugging time and make your system safer when actuators are involved. As you prototype, test each layer independently: verify Arduino output, confirm Pi can read it, then wire the web UI or control flows. The goal is to make incremental, testable steps that lead to a reliable IoT gateway pairing in a real deployment. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Quick Reference
Check devices
Confirm /dev nodes, i2cdetect output, and rfcomm connections before running code.
Use delimiters
Start/end markers or newlines prevent misaligned parsing when streams interleave.
Verify checksums
A simple XOR checksum flags corrupted payloads before acting on them.
Final tip
Build and verify each layer in order: Arduino output, Pi parsing, transport configuration, then UI and commands. That sequence keeps troubleshooting fast.
